new_head_para: Knowing this clearly, then, Hannibal urged Antiochus that, so long as he was planning anything hostile against the Romans, he should take heart and trust him, considering that he had in Hannibal a most genuine ally; but that if ever Antiochus should make a settlement or friendship with them, then he need wait for no slander, but should distrust Hannibal and be on his guard against him, for there was nothing Hannibal would not do against the Romans, if it lay in his power. Antiochus, hearing this and judging that it had been spoken with real feeling and sincerity, set aside all the suspicion he had held before.

new_head_para: At this same moment he himself, taking first the heavy infantry, behind them the cavalry, next the booty, and after all the rest the Iberians and Gauls, came to the narrows and the defiles. As for the Romans guarding the narrows, the moment they saw the lights advancing toward the heights, they supposed Hannibal was making his push that way, and so they abandoned the difficult ground and hurried to the help of the heights.
note: Greek is ἀναλαβὼν ... ἧκε: one participle, one verb. Joined English has 'moved out' plus 'he came' with no conjunction.
